claims.text: A conventionally tempered martensitic low-alloy steel can exhibit a ductile–brittle–ductile transition.
Systematic adjustment of tempering temperature and time can produce a narrow temperature window of temper embrittlement.
Accelerated carbide precipitation contributes to temper embrittlement in the proposed steel.
Impurity segregation contributes to temper embrittlement in the proposed steel.
The initial material is a conventional low-alloy martensitic steel in an as-quenched, hardened state.
Low tempering temperatures preserve ductile behavior.
An intermediate, narrow tempering-temperature range causes embrittlement.
Ductility is recovered at higher tempering temperatures.
Carbide precipitation dynamics and grain-boundary impurity segregation are the structural mediators of the transition.
Intermediate-temperature tempering promotes rapid carbide formation.
Intermediate-temperature tempering promotes impurity segregation at grain boundaries.
Carbide formation and grain-boundary impurity segregation temporarily embrittle the steel.
Further increasing the tempering temperature dissolves or redistributes the embrittling phases.
Dissolution or redistribution of the embrittling phases restores ductility.
Mechanical testing will reveal a pronounced ductility loss in a narrow intermediate-temperature window, flanked by ductile behavior at lower and higher temperatures.
The proposed behavior applies under conventional tempering regimes for low-alloy martensitic steels.
Temper embrittlement is absent from compositionally complex or high-entropy alloys.
The temperature window and magnitude of the ductility loss depend on alloy composition and heat-treatment kinetics.
Variations in impurity concentration can affect the transition.
